Jewish divorce, called gerushin, is the legal dissolution of a Jewish marriage according to halakha, Jewish law. The dissolution requires a get, a bill of divorce—a formal legal document written by a sofer, a trained Jewish scribe, and delivered by the husband to the wife in front of two valid witnesses. Both parties must accept the get willingly for the divorce to be valid according to Jewish law.

The get is a precise legal document written in Aramaic following a strict halakhic formula. Any significant error in the document renders it invalid. A sofer writes the get, and a beit din, a rabbinic court, supervises the process to ensure its validity. This careful scribal and judicial oversight reflects the seriousness with which Jewish law treats divorce and the importance of doing it correctly.

The husband must give the get to the wife of his own free will. A get given under coercion or extracted through duress is halakhically invalid, no matter what witnesses attest to it. Two valid witnesses must be present when the get is delivered and accepted. They sign the document to attest to the transaction.

The wife must physically receive and accept the get in front of witnesses. Without her acceptance, the marriage is not dissolved according to Jewish law. A woman cannot remarry according to Jewish law until she receives a valid get. Civil divorce alone does not dissolve the Jewish marriage in halakhic terms.

In Orthodox Judaism, remarriage before obtaining a valid get may result in mamzerut, illegitimate status, for any children born to a new union. Modern Jewish movements vary in their approach. Reform and Reconstructionist rabbis may recognize civil divorce, while Conservative Judaism typically requires a valid get even as it acknowledges civil law. These different approaches reflect varying understandings of how Jewish law relates to state law in matters of personal status and marriage.
